summary: notification-service is failing about 40% of SMS sends with "SMS provider returned 503", while e-mails are delivered normally. Users confirming a payment do not receive their one-time codes in roughly 40% of cases, so payment confirmation is blocked for a significant share of customers.

hypotheses.title: External SMS provider outage or degradation
hypotheses.reasoning: The 503 responses come from the SMS provider and only SMS is affected, while e-mail (a different external provider) works. This matches the known risk that notification-service degrades when external SMS/SMTP providers have issues. A partial failure rate of about 40% is consistent with provider-side instability or a partially unhealthy provider pool.
next_steps: Check the SMS provider's status page and any incident notices, and compare the start time with the first "SMS provider returned 503" entry in notification-service logs in ELK.
Query ELK for notification-service SMS send logs and break down failures by provider endpoint, destination country/operator and time to see whether the 503s are concentrated or uniform.
Check whether the provider supports a fallback route or secondary provider and whether notification-service can switch to it.

hypotheses.title: Rate limiting or overload on the provider side caused by our own traffic
hypotheses.reasoning: A 503 can be returned when the provider throttles or sheds load, which would explain why only a portion (about 40%) of sends fail. A spike in OTP requests, retries or duplicate sends from notification-service or payment-service could trigger this, and the start time is unknown.
next_steps: In ELK, chart the volume of SMS send requests from notification-service over the last several hours and look for a spike or retry storm that precedes the 503s.
Check payment-service logs for repeated OTP request calls per payment or user, which would indicate amplification.

hypotheses.title: Recent change in notification-service SMS integration
hypotheses.reasoning: The start time is unknown, so a deploy or config change (credentials, endpoint, request format, timeout or retry settings) cannot be ruled out. It would be distinguishable from a provider outage if only some instances or request types fail.
next_steps: Check the deployment and config change history for notification-service around the time the first 503s appeared.
Compare failure rates per notification-service instance in ELK; a failure confined to specific instances or versions points to our side rather than the provider.
Inspect the full 503 response body and headers in the logs for hints such as throttling or an upstream error message.
